newsitem.title: IRAN: Afghan talks end in Tehran without Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan talks end in Tehran without Taleban.

text.p: Afghan factions opposed to the Islamist Taleban militia ended a two-day conference in Tehran on Sunday with a call for an immediate ceasefire and an exchange of prisoners of war.
"Taleban missed their chance of an intra-Afghan dialogue for a peaceful settlement of the crisis," Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said.
"The participants called for an immediate ceasefire, the creation of a safe and secure environment in Kabul and the exchange of POWs," said a statement issued at the end of the talks.
"The sharing of power by all parties in the structure of the national government is indispensable."
The Taleban, who drove out president Burhanuddin Rabbani's government in September and now control two-thirds of Afghanistan, said on Friday they had not received any formal invitation for the talks.
A Taleban leader said in Kabul on Saturday that opposition groups must accept it as Afghanistan's government as a condition for peace talks and a ceasefire.

Rabbani, ousted prime minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and former president Sibghatullah Mojadedi took part in the Tehran meeting. The U.N. special envoy on Afghanistan and delegates from Pakistan, Turkey, Iran and Turkmenistan attended as observers.
Velayati said two official invitations were sent to the Taleban, who first said they were willing to come.
He suggested that the United States might have discouraged the Taleban from attending after U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Rafael met their leader in Islamabad last week.

Shi'ite Moslem Iran, which recognises Rabbani's government, has often criticised the Sunni Taleban for giving Islam a bad name. Iranian media have blasted the group, saying it was set up by Pakistan and backed by Washington. Pakistan denies the charge.
Iranian newspapers differed in their evaluation of the Tehran talks.
"Without Taleban, the meeting had no useful purpose other than to damage our national prestige in international political circles," the English-language Iran News said.
"The Tehran meeting has just been able to gather anti-Taleban forces. Perhaps it would result in a common strategy among Afghans," the daily Kayhan said.
"Any peace initiative taken by internationl organisations should be aimed at forcing the Taleban to give up their military strategy under military pressure," said the Tehran Times.
Attempts by the United Nations and Pakistan have failed to reconcile the Taleban and Rabbani's government. No country has formally recognised the Taleban government.
